ay9pkb:280: Traditional automated testing can only determine "whether functionality works" — an API returning 200 means success, a timeout means failure. But AI system outputs often involve dimensions that cannot be measured by binary judgment, such as content quality, expression fluency, and strategy reasonableness. The author introduced the Rubrics concept: for content quality evaluation scenarios, generate a series of evaluation cases at different levels (e.g., in an OKR query scenario, simply "whether results are retrieved or not" is lacking, but a series of different quality levels can be generated). This design solves the core challenge of AI evaluation: replacing subjective judgment with rule-based, structured evaluation sets. Each Rubrics dimension has clearly defined scoring criteria, and during evaluation, the AI only needs to determine "which level the current output corresponds to" — this is more reliable and more explainable than directly judging whether "the content is good or bad."

lsysq3:246: The pain point of traditional evaluation processes is not the process itself, but the lack of scalability of humans within it: evaluation set collection is time-consuming, evaluation execution burns time, and evaluators have low motivation. The AI First philosophy proposed by the author completely reverses this contradiction — instead of AI assisting humans in evaluation, it makes human intervention impossible from the entry level, with all evaluation actions completed autonomously by AI. The key to this shift lies in the paradigm change of "evaluation task description": humans only need to describe the evaluation goal ("comprehensively test DingTalk Docs MCP"), and the AI is responsible for decomposing it into specific evaluation cases, generating acceptance criteria, executing tests, and analyzing results. Throughout the process, humans don't need to know "what tools to use" or "which scenarios to cover" — the AI makes those judgments itself.
